idiom_name: tokio::sync::broadcast fan-out tap with Lagged-counted loss
implementation_notes: Rust has no EIP crate, so the tap is hand-wired from tokio's channel primitives; there are two realizations. Fan-out (several analyzers): tokio::sync::broadcast - the flow clones the Sender, each analyzer attaches with tap_tx.subscribe() without any change to sender or primary receiver, satisfying the insert/remove invariant. Thread model: Sender::send runs synchronously on the flow task and never blocks - it stores the value once in a ring buffer (the capacity argument is rounded up to the next power of two) and every Receiver later clones the value out at its own cursor, so analyzer work happens on each analyzer's own tokio::spawn task. Overflow policy is per receiver: once a receiver falls behind, the oldest unread values are overwritten and its recv() returns Err(RecvError::Lagged(n)) where n is the number of skipped messages - add n to a drop counter you export; the receiver is NOT disconnected, it resumes at the oldest retained value. Copy semantics: broadcast clones per receiver, so the copy is independent only if the payload's Clone is a deep copy - an Arc<T> field clones to the SAME heap allocation (zero-copy aliasing), so share immutable data, wrap in Arc::make_mut copy-on-write, or send a serialized Bytes snapshot. Point-to-point (one analyzer): bounded mpsc::channel(n) drained by a dedicated tap task; on the hot path call Sender::try_send(copy) and count drops on TrySendError::Full (the unsent value is returned, recoverable with into_inner) - awaiting Sender::send instead waits for capacity, which pulls the analyzer's latency into the flow and violates the out-of-band invariant. Note mpsc::Sender::clone is fan-IN (many producers, one consumer), so N analyzers need N channels - prefer broadcast beyond one tap. Non-async code uses the same shape with crossbeam-channel: bounded channel plus Sender::try_send, whose error distinguishes a full channel from a disconnected one; tokio's own mpsc docs point at crossbeam for sync-to-async bridging. Choose broadcast for multi-tap best-effort copies with Lagged-reported loss, bounded mpsc plus try_send for one tap with an explicit per-message accept/drop decision, and avoid unbounded channels when saturation must stay visible.
pitfalls: broadcast silently overwrites unread values: Receiver::recv returns Err(RecvError::Lagged(n)) only once the lag exceeds the effective capacity (the next power of two >= the capacity you passed - capacity 10 starts lagging past len 16), and a tap that unwraps recv or ignores the n loses exactly those messages unnoticed - count n and export it.

Sender::send's Ok(count) is a lie about delivery: the count is the number of subscribed Receiver handles, and docs state Ok does not mean any receiver observes the value while Err occurs only when ALL receivers are already dropped - a crashed, unsubscribed tap turns the wire tap into a silent no-op with no counter to observe.

Arc clone is zero-copy aliasing, not a copy: broadcast hands each receiver a clone of the stored value, but cloning a payload holding Arc<T> points at the same heap allocation (Arc::clone only bumps the atomic refcount), so an analyzer can observe primary-path mutations through Arc<Mutex<..>> or RwLock fields - deep-copy or serialize the snapshot.

Awaiting mpsc Sender::send on the flow task is in-band dispatch: the bounded channel's send 'waits until a message is received', so a stalled analyzer's backpressure becomes message-flow latency - on the hot path use try_send and treat TrySendError::Full as a counted drop instead.

mpsc::unbounded_channel hides overload: its send 'will always complete immediately' with infinite capacity, so a slow analyzer shows up as unbounded memory growth instead of loss - a wire tap needs a bounded queue with an explicit drop or Lagged policy, and the same applies to unbounded crossbeam channels.
